h: Palmerston's follies and the view from the top
p: Fort Nelson is one of a chain of forts built along Portsdown Hill in the 1860s, when there were serious fears of a French invasion. They were designed to protect Portsmouth from an attack by land, and because the invasion never came, they became known as Palmerston's Follies, after the Prime Minister of the day. Knowing that story makes exploring the ramparts and tunnels all the more interesting.

Among the most impressive pieces in the artillery collection is Mallet's Mortar, a giant Victorian weapon that looks almost too big to be real. Standing next to it gives you a real sense of how ambitious, and sometimes slightly bonkers, military engineering could be.
Allow a couple of hours to see the galleries and explore the fort properly. Comfortable shoes help, as there's uneven ground, steps and tunnels to explore, and it can get breezy on top of the hill.
Kids who love a bit of adventure will enjoy exploring the underground passages and hunting out the biggest guns, so build in time for them to roam.

There's plenty of history close by. Portchester Castle, at the head of Portsmouth Harbour, is a remarkable site with Roman walls surrounding a medieval castle, and it's just down the hill. Other Palmerston forts, including Fort Widley, sit further along Portsdown Hill, so you can spot the line of defences as you drive along.
Portsmouth's Historic Dockyard, Gunwharf Quays and the Spinnaker Tower are a short drive away for a bigger day out on the coast.
